top_stories.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
top_stories.content: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today.The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factoryThe best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud.Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work.Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days.To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48.“I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.”From agent rosters to dynamic workflowsThe pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single age

items.content: Release: web-edit 0.1a0 I was working on a project from my phone using Codex Remote when I found myself wanting to edit a credentials file without round-tripping those credentials through the LLM itself. So... I had Codex and GPT-6 Astra Extra High build this Python web app which provides a web UI for viewing and editing files in a folder. It's intended to be run over Tailscale, so I can have an agent start this running and then edit files via my Tailscale network directly from my phone. Here's the interface for browsing files in a folder: Editing uses CodeMirror 6 - I was going to use Monaco but that still doesn't have a great mobile experience yet. items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.content: Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation: lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]] [*L for L in lists] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}] {*s for s in sets} # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}] {**d for d in dicts} # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling. Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside o
